    f: F,
    g: G,
) -> [Either](https://docs.rs/enum.Either.html)<M, S> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/either/lib.rs.html#560-569)

#### pub fn [map_either_with](https://docs.rs#method.map_either_with)<Ctx, F, G, M, S>(
    self,
    ctx: Ctx,
    f: F,
    g: G,
) -> [Either](https://docs.rs/enum.Either.html)<M, S> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

Similar to [ map_either](https://docs.rs/enum.Either.html#method.map_either), with an added context

`ctx` accessible to
both functions.```
use either::*;
let mut sum = 0;
// Both closures want to update the same value, so pass it as context.
let mut f = |sum: &mut usize, s: String| { *sum += s.len(); s.to_uppercase() };
let mut g = |sum: &mut usize, u: usize| { *sum += u; u.to_string() };
let left: Either<String, usize> = Left("loopy".into());
assert_eq!(left.map_either_with(&mut sum, &mut f, &mut g), Left("LOOPY".into()));
let right: Either<String, usize> = Right(42);
assert_eq!(right.map_either_with(&mut sum, &mut f, &mut g), Right("42".into()));
assert_eq!(sum, 47);
```
Apply one of two functions depending on contents, unifying their result. If the value is
`Left(L)` then the first function `f` is applied; if it is `Right(R)` then the second
function `g` is applied.

```
use either::*;
fn square(n: u32) -> i32 { (n * n) as i32 }
fn negate(n: i32) -> i32 { -n }
let left: Either<u32, i32> = Left(4);
assert_eq!(left.either(square, negate), 16);
let right: Either<u32, i32> = Right(-4);
assert_eq!(right.either(square, negate), 4);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/either/lib.rs.html#617-626)#### pub fn [either_with](https://docs.rs#method.either_with)<Ctx, F, G, T>(self, ctx: Ctx, f: F, g: G) -> T

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/either/lib.rs.html#617-626)

#### pub fn [either_with](https://docs.rs#method.either_with)<Ctx, F, G, T>(self, ctx: Ctx, f: F, g: G) -> T

Like [ either](https://docs.rs/enum.Either.html#method.either), but provide some context to whichever of the
functions ends up being called.

```
// In this example, the context is a mutable reference
use either::*;
let mut result = Vec::new();
let values = vec![Left(2), Right(2.7)];
for value in values {
    value.either_with(&mut result,
                      |ctx, integer| ctx.push(integer),
                      |ctx, real| ctx.push(f64::round(real) as i32));
}
assert_eq!(result, vec![2, 3]);
```
Returns `other` if the value is [ Left](https://docs.rs/enum.Either.html#variant.Left), otherwise returns the

[value of](https://docs.rs/enum.Either.html#variant.Right)

`Right``self`.Arguments passed to `left_and` are eagerly evaluated; if you are passing the
result of a function call, it is recommended to use [ left_and_then](https://docs.rs/enum.Either.html#method.left_and_then), which is
lazily evaluated.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-4)Examples

```
use either::*;
let left: Either<_, u32> = Left(123);
assert_eq!(left.left_and::<()>(Right(246)), Right(246));
assert_eq!(left.left_and(Left(246)), Left(246));
let right: Either<u32, _> = Right(123);
assert_eq!(right.left_and::<()>(Right(246)), Right(123));
assert_eq!(right.left_and(Left(246)), Right(123));
```
Returns `other` if the value is [ Right](https://docs.rs/enum.Either.html#variant.Right), otherwise returns the

[value of](https://docs.rs/enum.Either.html#variant.Left)

`Left``self`.Arguments passed to `right_and` are eagerly evaluated; if you are passing the
result of a function call, it is recommended to use [ right_and_then](https://docs.rs/enum.Either.html#method.right_and_then), which is
lazily evaluated.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-5)Examples

```
use either::*;

assert_eq!(right.right_and(Right(246)), Right(246));
assert_eq!(right.right_and::<()>(Left(246)), Left(246));
```

Unlike [ into_iter](https://docs.rs/enum.Either.html#method.into_iter), this does not require the

`Left` and `Right` iterators to have the same item type.```
use either::*;

assert_eq!(right.factor_into_iter().collect::<Vec<_>>(), vec![Right(0), Right(1)]);
```

Borrows an `Either` of `Iterator`s to be an `Iterator` of `Either`s

Unlike [ iter](https://docs.rs/enum.Either.html#method.iter), this does not require the

`Left` and `Right` iterators to have the same item type.```
use either::*;
let left: Either<_, Vec<u8>> = Left(["hello"]);
assert_eq!(left.factor_iter().next(), Some(Left(&"hello")));
let right: Either<[&str; 2], _> = Right(vec![0, 1]);
assert_eq!(right.factor_iter().collect::<Vec<_>>(), vec![Right(&0), Right(&1)]);
```

Mutably borrows an `Either` of `Iterator`s to be an `Iterator` of `Either`s

Unlike [ iter_mut](https://docs.rs/enum.Either.html#method.iter_mut), this does not require the

`Left` and `Right` iterators to have the same item type.```
use either::*;
let mut left: Either<_, Vec<u8>> = Left(["hello"]);
left.factor_iter_mut().for_each(|x| *x.unwrap_left() = "goodbye");
assert_eq!(left, Left(["goodbye"]));
let mut right: Either<[&str; 2], _> = Right(vec![0, 1, 2]);
right.factor_iter_mut().for_each(|x| if let Right(r) = x { *r = -*r; });
assert_eq!(right, Right(vec![0, -1, -2]));
```
Return left value or given value

Arguments passed to `left_or` are eagerly evaluated; if you are passing
the result of a function call, it is recommended to use
[ left_or_else](https://docs.rs/enum.Either.html#method.left_or_else), which is lazily evaluated.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-6)Examples

```
let left: Either<&str, &str> = Left("left");
assert_eq!(left.left_or("foo"), "left");
let right: Either<&str, &str> = Right("right");
assert_eq!(right.left_or("left"), "left");
```

Arguments passed to `right_or` are eagerly evaluated; if you are passing

```

Factors out a homogeneous type from an `Either` of [ Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html).

Here, the homogeneous type is the `Err` type of the [ Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html).

assert_eq!(right.factor_err(), Ok(Right(String::new())));
```
Factors out a homogeneous type from an `Either` of [ Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html).

Here, the homogeneous type is the `Ok` type of the [ Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html).

```
use either::*;
let left: Either<_, Result<u32, String>> = Left(Err(vec![0]));
assert_eq!(left.factor_ok(), Err(Left(vec![0])));
let right: Either<Result<u32, Vec<u8>>, _> = Right(Err(String::new()));
assert_eq!(right.factor_ok(), Err(Right(String::new())));
```

# for_both in either - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/either/^1.0/macro.for_both.html

```
macro_rules! for_both {
    ($value:expr, $pattern:pat => $result:expr) => { ... };
    ($name:ident => $result:expr) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Evaluate the provided expression for both [ Either::Left](https://docs.rs/enum.Either.html#variant.Left) and

[.](https://docs.rs/enum.Either.html#variant.Right)

`Either::Right`This macro is useful in cases where both sides of [ Either](https://docs.rs/enum.Either.html) can be interacted with
in the same way even though the don’t share the same type.

Syntax:

- `either::for_both!(`- *expression*- `,`- *pattern*- `=>`- *expression*- `)`
- `either::for_both!(`- *ident*- `=>`- *expression*- `)`

Unlike [ map_both!](https://docs.rs/macro.map_both.html), this macro converges both variants to the type returned by the expression.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use either::Either;
fn length(owned_or_borrowed: Either<String, &'static str>) -> usize {
    either::for_both!(owned_or_borrowed, s => s.len())
}
fn main() {
    let borrowed = Either::Right("Hello world!");
    let owned = Either::Left("Hello world!".to_owned());
    assert_eq!(length(borrowed), 12);
    assert_eq!(length(owned), 12);
}
```
```
use either::Either;
fn length(s: Either<String, Vec<u8>>) -> usize {
    either::for_both!(s => s.len())
}
fn main() {
    let string = Either::Left("Hello world!".to_owned());
    let bytes = Either::Right(b"Hello world!".to_vec());
    assert_eq!(length(string), 12);
    assert_eq!(length(bytes), 12);
}
```
